deep.reconstruction:
This page is a printed page (p. 57) of an arithmetic textbook. The bundle name suggests Christian Leiste's 'Arithmetik und Algebra', Wolfenbüttel. It carries no substantive Gaussian manuscript content. The marginal '1846 / 1420' visible at the left edge belongs to the facing leaf: the previous page's numerical work ends with 18460 and 1420.

(1) Alligation (mixing) problem, end of §133 α. One alloy is 15-lötig: 15 Lot silver and 1 Lot copper per Mark of 16 Lot (the first sort's description is on the previous printed page). The other is 10-lötig: 10 Lot silver and 6 Lot copper. We want one Mark (q = 1) of 13-lötig alloy. The data are a = 15, b = 10, c = 13.
- Let x be the amount of the first sort. Then [my notation] a·x + b·(q − x) = c·q, so x = q(c − b)/(a − b).
- This gives x = (13 − 10)·1/(15 − 10) = 3/5 Mark of the first sort, and q − x = 2/5 Mark of the second.
- Check by rule of three: 1 Mark : 3/5 Mark = 15 Lot : 15·3/5 = 9 Lot of silver.
- Likewise 1 Mark : 2/5 Mark = 10 Lot : 10·2/5 = 4 Lot.
- The total is 9 + 4 = 13 Lot of silver per Mark.

(β) With three or more sorts: mix two of them in an arbitrary ratio and compute the value of that mixture by the weighted-mean rule (α). Treat this mixture as the sort b and proceed as before. Repeat until only two sorts remain.

(2) §134, Theorem (compound proportion). If a:b = c:d and m:n = p:q, then am:bn = cp:dq.
- Proof: b/a = d/c and n/m = q/p.
- Multiplying equals by equals (§17.2, §30.2) gives bn/(am) = dq/(cp).
- Hence am:bn = cp:dq.

(3) §135, Corollary.
- If n/m = b/a, then b²/a² = dq/(cp).
- If moreover q/p = d/c, then b²/a² = d²/c², i.e. a²:b² = c²:d². Hence also √a²:√b² = √c²:√d².
- Generalization: a:b = c:d implies a^m:b^m = c^m:d^m.
- Conversely, if A:B = C:D, then A^(1/m):B^(1/m) = C^(1/m):D^(1/m).
- The page ends with the catchword '§. 136.'; the next page treats the chain rule (Kettenregel).
errors: In §135 the print has '√a² : √b² : √c² : √d²'; the second colon should be '=' (√a²:√b² = √c²:√d²). This is a typographical slip.
In the final line the separator between ᵐ√C and ᵐ√D looks like a dot; it should be ':'.
§135 is logically trivial or circular. Setting m:n = a:b and p:q = c:d just multiplies the proportion by itself. The roots and m-th roots require positive quantities, which is implicit.

§133 β is incomplete as a method. The problem with three or more sorts is indeterminate, so infinitely many mixtures work. Also, the arbitrary pre-mixture must have a value such that the target c lies between it and the remaining sort; otherwise the two-sort rule gives a negative amount. The text does not mention this condition.
§134 tacitly assumes all terms are nonzero, since it divides by a, m, c, p.
